title: Supervised Learning
body:
Learning from **labelled** examples: every training row comes with the answer attached, and the
job is to produce a function that gets the answer right on rows it has never seen.

```
training data:  (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), … (xₙ, yₙ)      x = features, y = the answer
learn:          f  such that  f(xᵢ) ≈ yᵢ
use:            f(x_new)                             on data with no label
```

The labels are the supervision, and getting them is usually the expensive part of the whole
project. [[MNIST]] exists because someone hand-labelled 70,000 digits.

## Two kinds, by what $y$ is

| $y$ is | Task | Vault notes |
|---|---|---|
| a number | **regression** | [[Linear Regression]] |
| a category | **classification** | [[Logistic Regression]], [[Decision Tree]], [[Random Forest]], [[Classification]] |

The split matters because it decides the loss and the evaluation. Regression measures error as a
distance ([[Loss Function]]); classification counts right and wrong and then discovers that
counting is not enough, which is what [[Confusion Matrix]], [[Sensitivity]], and [[Specificity]]
are for.

## The one loop underneath all of them

1. Choose a **model** with adjustable parameters ([[Weights]]).
2. Choose a **[[Loss Function]]** measuring how wrong its predictions are.
3. **Minimise the loss** over the parameters, usually by [[Gradient Descent]].
4. Check on data the model has never seen.

Step 4 is the one beginners skip and the only one that tells the truth. **Fitting the training
data is not the goal**; a model with enough parameters can memorise it perfectly and be useless.
[[Bias]] carries the bias-variance trade that describes this, and [[Decision Tree]] is where the
vault shows it happening.

Steps 1 to 3 are the whole of [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and are written there and in `Books/`; this
note is the frame rather than a second treatment.

## Against the other two paradigms

| | Given | Learns from | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Supervised** | labelled examples | the right answer | is this digit a 7 |
| **[[Unsupervised Learning]]** | unlabelled data | structure in the data itself | which customers resemble each other |
| **[[Reinforcement Learning]]** | an environment | a delayed scalar reward | how to play the game |

Reinforcement learning is the interesting contrast. Supervised learning is told the correct action
for every situation; RL is told only a number, sometimes much later, and has to work out which of
its actions earned it. That is the credit-assignment problem and it is why RL is harder than it
looks from here.
